short_title: CMBS vs Life Company for Office and Retail
h1: CMBS vs Life Company for Office and Retail: How to Choose

seo.title: CMBS vs Life Company for Office and Retail Financing | Commercial Lending Solutions
seo.meta_description: CMBS conduit vs life insurance company loans for office and retail: current rate ranges, leverage, DSCR, prepayment, servicing and the decision rules that pick the lender.

lead: Office and retail commercial mortgages outside of agency come almost entirely from two channels: CMBS conduit pools and life insurance company balance sheets. CMBS provides leverage and flexibility for transitional and Class B properties; life company debt provides the lowest pricing on Class A properties with strong sponsors. As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows CMBS at 6.41 to 7.41 percent and life company loans at 6.10 to 6.70 percent across property types. CMBS reaches about 70 percent LTV on stabilized retail and 60 to 65 percent on office; life companies cap at 60 to 65 percent on the best retail and 55 to 60 percent on Class A office. The decision is rarely about price alone. It is about leverage, sponsor profile and how the asset will be managed through the loan term.

table.side_b: 6.10 to 6.70 percent, all property types

when_a_intro: CMBS wins on office and retail when the deal needs leverage that life co will not provide, when the property has Class B or transitional characteristics, or when the loan size is below the life co minimum. CMBS is the primary path for the broad middle of the office and retail market.
when_a_bullets: Class B office or retail where life co allocators will not lend at any price
Transitional asset with rollover risk where CMBS structural reserves provide a workable path
Loan size $5M to $10M which is below most life co minimums
Sponsor without an established life co relationship
Tertiary market where life co appetite is absent
Sponsor needs 65 to 70 percent leverage that life co will not provide on retail; 60 to 65 percent on office
when_b_intro: Life company wins on Class A office and retail when the leverage premium is acceptable, the sponsor profile fits the life co relationship tier, and the asset has the tenant credit quality and WALT to clear life co underwriting. The pricing compression on Class A is meaningful: 50 to 100 basis points inside CMBS.
when_b_bullets: Class A office in a top CBD or trophy retail with credit tenancy and long WALT
Sponsor with a deep CRE track record and an established life co relationship
Loan size $10M to $50M, which is life co's sweet spot
Borrower wants 15 to 25 year fixed term certainty that CMBS does not offer
Sponsor values direct lender servicing over CMBS pool servicing
Property in a primary market where life co allocator concentration is meaningful
decision_framework: On office, the asset class itself determines the lender pool. Trophy office in a top CBD with long-WALT credit tenancy is the only office product life cos will quote competitively today. Class B office, suburban office, and shorter-WALT office are CMBS or specialty debt fund territory. The post-COVID office market has bifurcated more than any other product type, and the lender ecosystem has bifurcated with it.

On retail, the segmentation is by asset type. Grocery-anchored shopping centers and credit STNL (drug stores, dollar stores, QSR) are competitive across both CMBS and life co. Power centers, lifestyle centers, and unanchored strip retail skew toward CMBS or specialty lenders because life cos have largely retreated from non-credit retail post-2020.

Leverage is the second axis. CMBS will quote 65 to 70 percent LTV on stabilized retail and 60 to 65 percent on stabilized office. Life cos cap retail at 60 to 65 percent and office at 55 to 60 percent. If the sponsor needs leverage above the life co cap, CMBS is the only path.

Servicing dynamics matter on long holds. CMBS loans are serviced under Pooling and Servicing Agreements that constrain post-close consents; minor lease modifications and tenant replacements can require formal servicer reviews. Life co loans are serviced directly by the lender and provide far more flexibility post-close. For sponsors planning active management, life co is materially easier to work with.

Five rules settle most office and retail decisions. One: if the asset is Class B, suburban or has a short weighted average lease term, plan on CMBS or debt fund execution. Two: if the property is Class A or credit anchored with a long WALT and the sponsor is established, get a life company quote first. Three: if you need more than 60 percent leverage on office or more than 65 percent on retail, CMBS is the only path of the two. Four: if you may sell or refinance within five years, compare the exit cost (defeasance or yield maintenance) before the coupon, because the cheaper coupon can lose to the cheaper exit. Five: if you plan active leasing and tenant changes, favor the lender whose consent process you can live with. Direct life company servicing is usually easier to work with than a master servicer.
real_deal_example: Consider a $30M grocery-anchored retail center, 95 percent occupied, with a 12-year weighted average lease term to a national chain anchor. A CMBS quote at 65 percent LTV is $19.5M at 7.15 percent fixed for 10 years, with defeasance and master servicer consent on lease changes. A life company quote at 60 percent LTV is $18.0M at 6.45 percent fixed for 15 years, with yield maintenance and direct lender servicing. On interest alone the life company loan costs about $233K less per year ($1.161M against $1.394M), but it delivers $1.5M less in proceeds. A sponsor who needs the extra proceeds takes CMBS. A sponsor who values the lower carry, the longer fixed term and an easier consent process takes the life company. The numbers only decide the question once the sponsor says which of those matters more.
expert_quote: On Class A retail and office, life co will price 50 to 100 basis points inside CMBS for the right sponsor. On Class B and transitional, life cos are not even at the table. The asset profile picks the lender; the sponsor profile picks the pricing tier.

faqs.q: Are life companies still lending on office in 2026?
faqs.a: Yes, but selectively. Life co allocators will lend on Class A office in top CBDs with strong sponsors, long WALT (12+ years), and credit tenancy. Life cos have largely exited Class B and suburban office. CMBS is the primary path for office that does not meet life co's narrow box.

faqs.q: What property types do life companies prefer in retail?
faqs.a: Grocery-anchored shopping centers, single-tenant net lease (STNL) with investment-grade tenants, and trophy lifestyle and power centers in primary markets. Life cos have largely retreated from unanchored strip retail and non-credit STNL post-2020.

faqs.q: How much cheaper is life company financing than CMBS on Class A retail?
faqs.a: On stabilized Class A grocery-anchored or credit-tenanted retail, life co typically prices 50 to 100 basis points inside comparable CMBS execution. The pricing advantage is most pronounced at 55 to 65 percent LTV with strong sponsors and long WALT.

faqs.q: Can CMBS lend at higher leverage than life co?
faqs.a: Yes. CMBS will quote 65 to 70 percent LTV on stabilized retail and 60 to 65 percent on stabilized office. Life co allocators typically cap retail at 60 to 65 percent and office at 55 to 60 percent. CMBS is the leverage leader on these product types.

faqs.q: What is WALT and why does it matter for life co underwriting?
faqs.a: WALT is weighted average lease term. Life co allocators size loans against the weighted average remaining lease term across the rent roll, with a strong preference for 10+ year WALT on retail and office. Properties with shorter WALT face proceeds reductions or are declined entirely under life co programs.

faqs.q: Can a CMBS loan be assumed by a buyer?
faqs.a: Most CMBS loans are assumable subject to lender approval and a 1 percent assumption fee. Assumption is one of CMBS's structural advantages over yield maintenance prepayment, since it preserves the loan in place and avoids YM costs at sale. Life co loans are also typically assumable but require direct lender approval.

faqs.q: How does CMBS handle tenant rollover on office and retail?
faqs.a: CMBS loans on office and retail typically include cash-managed reserves and structural triggers tied to tenant credit, lease term, and DSCR. Tenant rollover within the loan term often triggers a cash sweep that diverts excess cash to leasing reserves until re-leasing is achieved. These provisions are heavily negotiated in CMBS B-piece due diligence and are often the most important structural points for the sponsor.

faqs.q: Are life co office loans non-recourse?
faqs.a: Yes. Life co office and retail loans are structurally non-recourse with bad-boy carve-outs, identical to CMBS and agency on the recourse axis. The lender's protection on office is leverage discipline (55 to 60 percent LTV) and tenant credit quality, not recourse to the sponsor.

faqs.q: What do CMBS and life company loans cost right now?
faqs.a: As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows CMBS at 6.41 to 7.41 percent and life company loans at 6.10 to 6.70 percent, before property, sponsor and structure adjustments. Life company debt is usually cheaper on the assets it will lend on, and CMBS reaches the assets and leverage levels life companies will not.

faqs.q: Can I put mezzanine debt or a second loan behind a CMBS or life company loan?
faqs.a: Usually only with the senior lender's consent and an intercreditor agreement, and CMBS documents restrict secondary financing more tightly than most life company documents. If extra leverage is the goal, plan the capital stack before choosing the senior lender, and compare the structure against bridge or mezzanine alternatives.

faqs.q: Which closes faster, CMBS or a life company?
faqs.a: Both typically close in 60 to 90 days. Life company timing depends on allocation and the path from quote to term sheet. CMBS timing depends on the rate lock, third-party reports and the securitization calendar. Clean financials and early third-party reports save more time than the choice of lender type.

h1: Bridge Loan vs Permanent Refinance: Reposition First or Lock Rate Now

seo.title: Bridge Loan vs Permanent Refinance for Commercial Real Estate | Commercial Lending Solutions
seo.meta_description: Bridge loan or permanent refinance? Current rate ranges, proceeds basis, speed, the stabilization gap test and a worked scenario for when bridging first pays.

lead: A bridge loan wins when the property is not yet earning what it can and a permanent loan today would be sized on income you have not yet created. A permanent refinance wins when the property is stabilized and the goal is the lowest cost with years of rate certainty. As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows bridge debt at 7.75 to 11.75 percent and permanent debt at 5.91 to 8.16 percent across lender types. Bridge lenders size on as-is value and the business plan, usually close in weeks, and expect a refinance or sale within 12 to 36 months. Permanent lenders size on in-place net operating income, take 60 to 90 days, and lock a fixed rate for 5 to 30 years. The test is the stabilization gap: if the extra proceeds at stabilized value exceed the extra cost of bridging, bridge first.

table.side_a: Debt funds, mortgage REITs, private credit, select banks
table.side_b: Life insurance companies, agency (Fannie and Freddie), CMBS conduits, banks

table.side_a: As-is value plus a future-funding component for capex and lease-up
table.side_b: In-place stabilized net operating income and trailing performance

table.side_a: 7.75 to 11.75 percent, typically floating over SOFR
table.side_b: 5.91 to 8.16 percent across agency, life company, CMBS and bank lenders

table.side_a: Often 2 to 6 weeks when the story is clear
table.side_b: Typically 60 to 90 days; HUD and FHA take longer

table.side_b: 60 to 75 percent of stabilized value, amortizing

table.side_a: 12 to 36 months plus extensions
table.side_b: 5, 7, 10 years or longer

table.side_a: Open after a short lockout
table.side_b: Yield maintenance or defeasance on agency and CMBS

table.side_a: Non-recourse with carve-outs common; partial recourse on heavier plans
table.side_b: Non-recourse on agency, CMBS, and most life company

table.side_b: Stabilized occupancy and NOI, no further upside to chase, rate certainty wanted

when_a_intro: A bridge loan wins when the property is not yet performing at its potential and refinancing today would lock in proceeds based on depressed or transitional income.
when_a_bullets: Occupancy is below market and a credible lease-up or renovation plan will lift NOI within 12 to 24 months
In-place DSCR is below the 1.20x to 1.25x that permanent lenders require to size full proceeds
An existing loan is maturing before the business plan is complete and a short extension is not available
The sponsor wants flexibility to sell or recapitalize once value is created rather than locking long-term debt
Recent capex or repositioning is not yet reflected in the trailing financials a permanent lender underwrites
when_b_intro: A permanent refinance wins when the asset is stabilized and the goal is the lowest cost of capital with long-term rate certainty.
when_b_bullets: Occupancy and NOI are stabilized and trailing performance supports full permanent proceeds
There is little remaining value-add upside, so paying bridge pricing to chase it is not justified
The sponsor expects to hold and wants to lock a fixed rate against future rate risk
Cash-out at today's stabilized value already meets the sponsor's return on equity
The asset qualifies for agency or life company execution at the tightest available spreads
decision_framework: Measure the stabilization gap: compare in-place NOI to credible stabilized NOI. A wide gap favors bridge; a narrow gap favors permanent now.

Weigh the upside against the carry: if the incremental proceeds at stabilized value exceed the extra interest and fees of bridging, the bridge pays for itself. The worked scenario below shows the arithmetic.

Build the plan backward from the refinance. A bridge only works if a named permanent lender type will take it out, so identify the take-out first (agency, life company or CMBS), note the occupancy and trailing income it requires, usually stabilized occupancy near 90 percent with several months of steady collections, and confirm the bridge term and extension options give you enough runway to reach it.

Factor the rate view and hold period: a sponsor who wants certainty and a long hold leans permanent; one who plans to sell or recapitalize after value creation leans bridge. Never choose a bridge simply because the permanent quote looks tight, and never choose permanent simply because the coupon looks low if it leaves value on the table.
real_deal_example: Consider a 140-unit apartment community at 82 percent occupancy after deferred maintenance, worth $21M as is and $27M once renovated and leased up. A permanent loan sized today at 60 percent of as-is value is about $12.6M at 6.50 percent. A bridge at 75 percent of as-is value is about $15.75M at 8.75 percent, interest only. Over 24 months the bridge interest is about $2.76M against about $1.64M on the permanent loan, roughly $1.1M of added carry before fees. At stabilization, an agency refinance at 70 percent of $27M is about $18.9M, which repays the bridge and leaves about $3.15M, compared with about $12.6M available from refinancing today. If the extra proceeds and the value created are worth more than $1.1M of carry plus fees, the bridge wins. If the renovation will not reach the stabilized income, the permanent loan wins.
expert_quote: The mistake is refinancing into permanent debt the day before you execute the plan that creates the value. If there is real upside left, a bridge sized on as-is value with room to capture it usually beats locking proceeds on income you have not earned yet.

faqs.q: Can I refinance a bridge loan into a permanent loan later?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the intended exit for most bridge loans. The bridge carries the property through lease-up or renovation, then a permanent loan from a life company, agency lender, or CMBS conduit takes out the bridge at the higher stabilized value once the business plan is complete.

faqs.q: Why not just refinance into permanent debt now and avoid bridge pricing?
faqs.a: If the property is stabilized, that is usually the right call. The bridge only makes sense when refinancing today would size proceeds on transitional income, leaving value on the table that a short bridge lets you capture before the permanent take-out.

faqs.q: How much more does a bridge loan cost than permanent financing?
faqs.a: Bridge debt typically prices several hundred basis points wider than permanent, plus origination and exit fees. The decision is whether the additional proceeds and flexibility created by repositioning exceed that incremental cost over the bridge term.

faqs.q: What DSCR do permanent lenders require to size full proceeds?
faqs.a: Most permanent lenders look for stabilized debt service coverage around 1.20x to 1.25x or better on in-place income. A property below that threshold often cannot support full permanent proceeds, which is where a bridge to stabilization comes in.

faqs.q: How long does a bridge loan last?
faqs.a: Most bridge loans run 12 to 36 months, often with one or two extension options that carry an extension fee and sometimes a performance test. Plan the take-out so it happens with room to spare before the final maturity, not on the last day.

faqs.q: What occupancy do I need before refinancing out of a bridge?
faqs.a: Permanent lenders generally want to see stabilized occupancy, commonly around 90 percent or higher, and several months of steady collections at the new rents. The exact bar depends on the property type, the lender and the program, so ask the take-out lender early, not at maturity.

faqs.q: What do bridge and permanent loans cost today?
faqs.a: As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows bridge debt at 7.75 to 11.75 percent and permanent debt at 5.91 to 8.16 percent across lender types, before property, sponsor and structure adjustments. The gap in cost is the price of flexibility and as-is sizing.

faqs.q: Can I do both, bridge first and permanent after?
faqs.a: Yes. That two-stage plan is the standard way to capture value: a short bridge to execute the business plan, then a permanent take-out at stabilized value. The strategy only works when the take-out is planned from day one.

h1: CMBS vs Life Company vs Agency Debt: Which Permanent Loan Fits

seo.title: CMBS vs Life Company vs Agency Debt Compared | CLS CRE
seo.meta_description: CMBS, life insurance company and agency (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac) permanent loans side by side: current rate ranges, leverage, DSCR, prepayment, timing and when each one wins.

lead: Agency debt from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is the cheapest high-leverage choice, but only for multifamily and a few related residential property types. For every other stabilized property the choice is CMBS or a life insurance company: life company loans price lowest on high-quality assets with strong sponsors, and CMBS reaches higher leverage and more property types. As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows life companies at 6.10 to 6.70 percent, agency at 6.16 to 7.11 percent and CMBS at 6.41 to 7.41 percent. Choose by property type first, leverage second, sponsor profile third, and compare exit costs before you compare coupons.

when_a_intro: CMBS wins when leverage, property type or loan size rules out a life company and the property is not multifamily.
when_a_bullets: Office, retail, industrial or hotel property that does not meet the life company box
The sponsor needs more leverage than life companies offer
The loan is sized below life company minimums
The asset has some transition or tenant rollover that a life company will not underwrite
The sponsor accepts defeasance and master servicing in exchange for proceeds
when_b_intro: A life company wins when the asset and sponsor are strong enough to earn the lowest coupon and the sponsor wants a long fixed term.
when_b_bullets: Stabilized, high-quality property with long leases or strong multifamily fundamentals
A sponsor with a track record and moderate leverage needs
Borrower wants 15 to 25 years of fixed-rate certainty
Direct lender servicing and consent flexibility matter for an actively managed asset
Multifamily at lower leverage, where a life company can price inside agency execution
when_c_intro: Agency debt wins on stabilized multifamily when leverage and cost matter most.
when_c_bullets: Multifamily with 5 or more units, or a related residential program such as senior or student housing
The sponsor wants leverage up to 80 percent, or up to 85 percent through HUD programs
Affordable and workforce programs where Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac offer specialized execution
A supplemental loan later is part of the business plan
The sponsor wants non-recourse debt that is assumable with lender approval
decision_framework: Start with property type. Multifamily gives you all three options. Every other property type is CMBS or a life company, because agency lending is limited to multifamily and a few related programs.

Then look at leverage. Agency debt reaches up to 80 percent, CMBS reaches 60 to 75 percent depending on property type, and life companies usually stop at 55 to 65 percent. If the sponsor needs the proceeds, leverage often decides before price does.

Then look at the asset and the sponsor. Life companies pay for quality with a lower coupon and pass on assets they do not like. CMBS and agency lenders accept more variety and rely on structure (reserves, cash management, DSCR tests) to manage the risk.

Compare exit costs, not just coupons. CMBS usually means lockout and defeasance, life companies usually mean yield maintenance, and agency loans usually mean yield maintenance or a step-down. If you may sell or refinance within five years, the cheaper coupon can lose to the cheaper exit.

A practical shortcut. For multifamily of $2M or more, get an agency quote first and use a life company quote as the price check. For Class A or credit-tenant property above $10M, get a life company quote first and use CMBS as the leverage check. For everything else that is not multifamily, start with CMBS and see whether a life company will do the deal at a lower rate.

Costs people miss. CMBS often brings single-purpose borrower requirements, cash management and servicing fees. Life company rate locks often require a good-faith deposit that can be forfeited if you walk. Agency loans carry lender and agency fees and third-party reports. Ask each lender for a full cost sheet before comparing.
example_title: The Same $25M Apartment Building, Three Quotes
real_deal_example: Consider a stabilized apartment building worth $25M. An agency quote at 75 percent LTV is $18.75M at 6.50 percent. A CMBS quote at 70 percent LTV is $17.5M at 6.90 percent. A life company quote at 60 percent LTV is $15.0M at 6.30 percent. On interest alone the life company loan is cheapest at about $945K a year, against about $1.219M for agency and $1.208M for CMBS. But agency delivers $3.75M more proceeds than the life company loan for about $274K more interest, which prices that extra capital at roughly 7.3 percent. If the sponsor needs the capital, agency wins. If the sponsor wants the lowest carry and does not need the proceeds, the life company wins. CMBS rarely wins on stabilized multifamily when agency is available.
example_note: This is an illustrative scenario with round numbers, not a specific CLS CRE closing. Actual terms depend on the property, sponsor and structure.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CMBS, life company and agency loans?
faqs.a: CMBS loans are pooled and sold to investors, so structure and servicing rules are rigid but leverage and property types are broad. Life company loans are held on the insurer's balance sheet, so pricing is low and servicing is direct but underwriting is selective. Agency loans are made under Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac programs for multifamily and carry the highest leverage and fastest timelines.

faqs.q: Which has the lowest rate, CMBS, life company or agency?
faqs.a: As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows life companies lowest at 6.10 to 6.70 percent, agency at 6.16 to 7.11 percent and CMBS at 6.41 to 7.41 percent. Life companies only lend on the strongest assets and sponsors, so the lowest rate is not available on every deal.

faqs.q: Which is best for multifamily?
faqs.a: Agency debt is usually best for stabilized multifamily because it combines the highest leverage, competitive pricing and fast timelines. A life company can win at lower leverage and a longer fixed term, and CMBS rarely wins when agency is available.

faqs.q: Which is best for office, retail or industrial?
faqs.a: Agency lenders do not make these loans. Life companies are the low-cost choice for Class A and credit-tenant property with long leases and strong sponsors. CMBS is the usual path for everything else, especially when leverage matters or the asset has transition risk.

faqs.q: Which gives the highest leverage?
faqs.a: Agency debt, at up to 80 percent LTV on multifamily and up to 85 percent through HUD programs. CMBS typically reaches 60 to 75 percent depending on property type, and life companies usually stop at 55 to 65 percent.

faqs.q: How do prepayment penalties differ?
faqs.a: CMBS loans usually have a lockout followed by defeasance, which replaces the loan with a portfolio of securities and can be costly when rates fall. Life company loans usually use yield maintenance. Agency loans use yield maintenance or a declining step-down. Compare the cost of exit at your likely sale or refinance date.

faqs.q: Are these loans recourse?
faqs.a: All three channels are generally non-recourse with standard carve-outs for fraud, misapplied funds, bankruptcy and similar events. Individual programs differ, so confirm the guaranty terms in the term sheet.

faqs.q: Can a broker compare all three for my property?
faqs.a: Yes. CLS CRE arranges loans from $2 million to $100 million and up through more than 1,000 lenders, and will run your property past CMBS, life company and agency lenders and send side-by-side terms.

h1: Commercial Mortgage Broker vs Bank: Which Gets You the Better Loan

seo.title: Commercial Mortgage Broker vs Bank: Pros and Cons | CLS CRE
seo.meta_description: Should you use a commercial mortgage broker or go straight to a bank? Lender access, pricing, recourse, speed, fees and when each is the better choice, with current rate ranges.

lead: A bank is one lender with one balance sheet, one credit box and one price. A commercial mortgage broker takes the same deal to many lenders (banks, life companies, agencies, CMBS and debt funds) and negotiates among them. Go direct to a bank when the loan is small, the property is simple and you already have a deposit relationship. Use a broker when the loan is $2 million or more, the deal has a wrinkle such as transition, leverage, recourse or speed, or you want to know the bank's offer is the best available. The broker's cost is a fee. The bank's cost is the offer you never see. As of November 24, 2026, the CLS CRE rate table shows permanent loans at 5.91 to 8.16 percent across all lender types and bank portfolio loans at 6.91 to 8.16 percent.

rate_note: Program ranges come from the CLS CRE rate table, last changed November 24, 2026, and are built from current Treasury, SOFR and prime benchmarks. Pricing depends on the property, sponsor and structure.
when_a_intro: A broker wins when the value of seeing the whole market is larger than the broker's fee, which is most commercial loans of $2 million and above.
when_a_bullets: The loan is $2 million or more and the property or sponsor has any complication
You need non-recourse debt, higher leverage or a longer fixed term than banks offer
The property is in transition, or the bank has declined or slow-walked the deal
You are time-constrained and need several lenders working in parallel
You want to know whether the bank's offer is competitive before you sign it
You are buying or refinancing outside the lenders you already know
when_b_intro: Going direct wins when the loan is simple and your bank already values the relationship.
when_b_bullets: The loan is under $2 million, below where CLS CRE works
Your bank already knows the property and will price your deposits into the loan
The deal is low leverage, short term and fits the bank's credit box cleanly
You prefer one point of contact and the bank's terms are clearly competitive
A local construction or bridge need where the bank's own balance sheet is the natural fit
decision_framework: The real comparison is access against a fee. A bank can only offer what its own balance sheet wants, while a broker can show you what the wider market offers. The fee is only worth paying if the broker finds a better rate, higher proceeds, a better structure or a faster close.

The simplest test is to get your bank's term sheet first, then ask a broker to beat or match it. If the bank wins, you have lost nothing but a little time and you can close with confidence. If the broker wins, the savings usually exceed the fee.

Ask any broker five questions before you sign. How are you paid, and who pays you? Which lenders will you actually approach for this deal? Have you closed loans like mine in the last year? Is the engagement exclusive, and for how long? What happens to your fee if I take the bank's offer instead?
We are a broker, so weigh our view accordingly. The way to check it is to compare real offers side by side, not to trust any broker's claim, including ours.

faqs.q: Does a commercial mortgage broker cost more than going to a bank?
faqs.a: A broker adds a fee, but the fee is often offset by a lower rate, higher proceeds or better terms found by comparing lenders. A bank charges its own fees but has no one comparing alternatives for you. The right answer depends on how much the better offer is worth on your loan size.

faqs.q: How do commercial mortgage brokers get paid?
faqs.a: Compensation is agreed in writing before work starts and is commonly a percentage of the loan, paid at closing, sometimes by the borrower, sometimes by the lender, sometimes shared. Always ask who pays, how much and what happens if the loan does not close.

faqs.q: Can a broker get a better rate than my bank?
faqs.a: Often, because a broker can reach lenders your bank cannot, such as life companies, agencies and CMBS, but not always. If your bank has a deposit relationship and a simple deal, it can win. The way to know is to compare a real bank term sheet with the brokered offers.

faqs.q: Does a broker shopping my deal hurt my credit?
faqs.a: Commercial loan shopping generally does not involve repeated personal credit pulls the way consumer mortgage shopping does, but practices vary. Ask your broker how your information is shared and when credit is actually run.

faqs.q: When should I go straight to my bank?
faqs.a: When the loan is small, the property is simple, the bank already knows you and its terms are clearly competitive. Also when you value one point of contact more than a possible rate improvement.

faqs.q: Does CLS CRE work on small loans?
faqs.a: CLS CRE arranges commercial mortgage loans from $2 million to $100 million and up. For smaller loans, a local bank or credit union is usually the better starting point.

faqs.q: What should I ask before hiring a commercial mortgage broker?
faqs.a: Ask how they are paid and by whom, which lenders they will approach, whether they have closed similar loans recently, whether the engagement is exclusive and for how long, and what the fee is if you choose another lender. Our guide to choosing a broker covers the full checklist.
